Title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents
Abstract: Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input.A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can refire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks.Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured.We present Carryover Bench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced.A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages.Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection.Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions. 1
Major_Contribution_Result: CarryoverBench evaluates cross-session 'carryover' prompt injections that plant payloads into persistent memory or scheduled tasks and later re-fire. It includes 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across Instant, Autonomous (heartbeat), and Latent (memory) channels, with plant vs trigger scored separately by a rule-based verifier. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire over five rounds without measurable decay; once planting succeeds, the trigger stage often adds little protection. Porting Latent attacks to Hermes attenuates but does not eliminate ASR.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: Authors note three limitations: (1) the rule-based verifier can miss successful exfiltration if markers appear outside aliased role fields (ASR as relative signal); (2) Latent triggers replay identical follow-ups, so P(trig|plant) is an upper bound under topical alignment, not realistic multi-day diversity; (3) reasoning-model coverage is limited (Gemini-3.1-Pro in default reasoning; Hermes runtime ablation excludes it due to latency; separate Qwen reasoning probe in appendix).
Critics: Strong contribution for agent-security evaluation of stateful persistence channels that single-session IPI benchmarks miss. Results emphasize plant/trigger decomposition and runtime-layer failure modes. Verifier false negatives and Latent trigger design mean absolute ASR should be interpreted cautiously; the work measures persistence more than proposing a complete defense.
